analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil taken from federal lands to guarantee funding for low-income home energy aid.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or a single cosponsor and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put a small tax — no more than 50 cents per barrel — on oil extracted from federal lands and offshore leases, and deposited the money into a dedicated trust fund for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which helps poor households pay heating and cooling bills. The fund could provide up to $5.1 billion a year, and the tax rate would automatically shrink if Congress already appropriated enough LIHEAP money in a given year. The lease holder — the oil company extracting the oil — would pay the tax. The bill was referred to three House committees in January 2012, sent to one subcommittee in March, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that receive LIHEAP help paying their heating and cooling bills. Instead of the program depending entirely on year-to-year congressional appropriations, the bill would give it a dedicated funding stream worth up to $5.1 billion a year, topped up by the oil tax only when regular appropriations fall short.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated LIHEAP Trust Fund in the Treasury, financed by a new tax on oil extracted from federal lands and offshore leases, so energy assistance for the poor would no longer depend solely on annual appropriations fights [S2][S3].
Caps the aid at $5.1 billion per fiscal year but automatically reduces the tax rate when Congress already appropriates enough LIHEAP money, avoiding over-collecting [S2][S3].

Sets the tax at the lesser of 50 cents per barrel or the amount needed to close the gap between $5.1 billion and regular appropriations, and charges it to the holder of the federal oil lease [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies that produce from federal lands and offshore leases, which would pay up to 50 cents per barrel. Some or all of that cost could be passed through to consumers as slightly higher fuel prices, and federal taxpayers would forgo a slice of existing federal oil revenue that is otherwise shared with the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The tax is paid by lease holders but its cost can be passed to consumers through fuel prices, so a share of the funding could come from the same households LIHEAP serves [S3].

The bill does not fully guarantee $5.1 billion: the special tax only applies in a fiscal year if Congress enacted a LIHEAP appropriation before the year began, and if it did not, the rate simply carries over from the prior year, leaving the program still partly hostage to the appropriations process [S3].

The tax diverts money from federal oil revenue otherwise shared with the Treasury, and at a maximum of 50 cents a barrel it is a modest funding fix rather than a solution to LIHEAP's larger shortfall [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: a guaranteed, automatic funding stream for a program that helps poor households survive winter heating and summer cooling bills. The cost is also narrow — up to 50 cents a barrel on federal-lease oil, part of which would likely show up in fuel prices. The design has a weakness: the guarantee only works if Congress passes the annual LIHEAP appropriation on time, so it does not fully remove the uncertainty it aims to fix. On balance it is a modest, reasonably targeted transfer from federal-lease oil production to low-income energy assistance.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee from the day it was introduced; the House never voted on it, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Murphy of Connecticut introduced the bill on January 23, 2012, and it was referred to three committees at once — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce [S1][S5].
On March 29, 2012 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Training, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill died without a vote when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies producing from federal lands and offshore leases never had to pay the new per-barrel tax, and LIHEAP funding stayed dependent on annual appropriations rather than a dedicated revenue stream.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal-lease oil producers, not LIHEAP households

for.name: Rep. Christopher Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three House committees.

against.name: Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the primary committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded vote, so no partisan breakdown exists in the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands and offshore leases
industries.note: The bill would charge lease holders up to 50 cents per barrel extracted from federal lands and offshore leases to fund energy aid for the poor. The per-barrel cost is small next to oil prices, but the industry's interest in the bill ran against the households it would have funded.

industries.industry: LIHEAP assistance recipients and state energy-aid programs
industries.note: A dedicated trust fund worth up to $5.1 billion a year would have made energy assistance for low-income households steadier and less dependent on annual congressional budget fights.
